title: Silver in a shell
hook: the king has just declared himself free, and the sage answers by asking why he still wants money
carry: wanting grows from forgetting the self

segments.voice: Yesterday, aho: Janaka's cry of wonder, and every wave is water: the self in everything. Every wave is water: the self in everything. Today, the teacher answers the cry.

What does a good teacher do when a student announces, I've got it? A whole chapter of joy has just poured out of King Janaka: spotless, at peace, salutation to me. Another book might end right there, the student shining and the teacher nodding. The Ashtavakra Gita doesn't. Chapter three opens with the sage leaning in, his tone almost dry. If you really know yourself as the one, imperishable Self, he asks, why are you still keen on piling up wealth? A question aimed straight at a king with a treasury, and at anyone who has made a big announcement about themselves.
screen: `I'VE GOT IT.` → `THE TEACHER LEANS IN.` → `THEN WHY STILL PILE UP WEALTH?`

segments.voice: Much of the third chapter is questions like that, in paraphrase. You know the Self as one and imperishable; why the hunger to get more? Then a picture. Someone on a beach sees a glint in a shell, takes the mother-of-pearl for silver, and a little greed wakes up. The greed is real. The silver isn't. In the same way, he says, wanting for the world rises out of not knowing the Self. That's one of the central teachings of Advaita, the non-dual school: the hunger to grab and hoard grows from forgetting what you are, the atman, already whole. Teachers call that forgetting avidya, not-knowing. Spotless and at peace are easy words to say. The test is whether the hand still closes around the silver. Ashtavakra isn't calling Janaka a liar. He's asking whether the knowing has reached his habits yet, or only his mouth. In the next chapter Janaka answers, calmly: the one who knows the Self moves through the world as though it were a game, not weighed down by it. He shows the sage where he stands. A claim, a test, an answer. In this tradition, knowing the Self shows in the hand, not only in the mouth. Someone who knows they're already whole doesn't need the shell to be silver.
screen: `THE TEACHER ANSWERS WONDER WITH A TEST.` · `SILVER IN A SHELL.` · `AVIDYA: WANTING GROWS FROM NOT KNOWING THE SELF.` · `HAS IT REACHED THE HABITS, OR ONLY THE MOUTH?` · then, large: `A CLAIM, A TEST, AN ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you've been reaching for lately: a purchase, a bit of praise, a result. Without judging it, look the way the sage looks at Janaka: silver, or a glint in a shell? Notice where the wanting sits in the body, the chest, the jaw, the hands. Then try the old Advaita move: the wanting is seen, and I am the one who sees it. If you pray, offer the wanting to God just as it is; either way, let the hand open a little.
Shukti. Mother-of-pearl, the shell mistaken for silver. In the Ashtavakra Gita, the sage tests the king by asking why he still reaches, like someone taking a shell for silver.
Your line: wanting grows from forgetting the self. Silver, or a shell? The hand will tell you. Until tomorrow.

screen: `DAY 1002 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: WHO IS THE GREAT IDLER?`

howItsDone: Some readers of the Ashtavakra Gita take chapters two, three and four together: Janaka's declaration, the sage's testing questions, and Janaka's calm reply, as a model of how a teacher checks a student's realization.

fork.setup: a friend comes home from a scripture class saying they're past wanting things, then spends the night on a sale. you're the sage. what do you do?
options: ask, kindly, why someone who knows the Self still reaches.
say nothing; wanting has nothing to do with the Self.
fork.reveal: Ashtavakra never calls Janaka a liar. he asks why one who knows the Self still reaches, because wanting grows from forgetting it.

Ashtavakra.meaning: the sage whose name means eight bends

Janaka.meaning: king of Videha, the sage's royal student

avidya.meaning: not-knowing: forgetting what you truly are

Advaita.meaning: non-dual: the school teaching that the Self and Brahman are one
